scenario: AITA for Seeking Prayers at a Scheduled Prayer Service? | Hello all. This week I was at a prayer service at my college fellowship. We have these once a week, and they are open to the public. A student at our school died recently in an accident, and so there were more people at the service than normal. Lots of people were crying. I did not know him, but I still prayed for him with everyone else. During the service, people offer up statements and some ask for prayers. This time, lots of people were remembering the student but a few people asked for prayers for sick relatives, one for her cousin who was struggling with drug addiction, and then it came to me. I broke up with my girlfriend of about 3 months two weeks ago, and it has been really tough on me. She was also at the prayer service even though she is not as Christian as I am and normally was not there. She just happened to know the student who passed away. I asked people to pray for me that I recover from my breakup and that in the future I only date people who truly share my religious values because those people would not be hurtful. Fast forward to that afternoon, I got messages from several of my friends telling me that asking for prayers, during a prayer service, was inconsiderate. My ex girlfriend also sent me a message telling me that she found it hurtful and that she would prefer that I not speak about her again, at least not when she is present. I asked her what was wrong with what I said, and she told me I was attacking her. I was not! I never attacked her. I understand that people there were suffering, but we all suffer for different reasons. I am also suffering. I have never had such a tragic breakup, and I thought she was the one who I would marry. I was already looking at rings, and then she just broke up with me. I have a right to be sad, don't I? I have a right to ask to be lifted in spirit--we all have different crosses to bear. A couple of my friends are not even talking to me. Am I really wrong here? I am interested in what you have to say.

Clean & Prepare the House (Most Critical First!)** - **Deep clean** high-traffic areas (living room, kitchen, guest rooms). - **Declutter** surfaces, floors, and entryways for a welcoming vibe. - **Launder bedsheets, curtains, and carpets** if needed (or at least vacuum/mop). - **Replace air filters** (if AC/heaters are running) for fresh air. ### **2. Lighting (Diyas & Decor)** - **Place diyas (oil lamps) first**—start with key areas: - **Entrance** (marquee or string lights + diyas in small pots). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Kitchen** (if open to guests) and **puja room** (if applicable). - **Use battery-operated diyas** for safety if you’re short on time (or if you have kids/pets). - **Add fairy lights** (string lights, LED garlands) for a soft glow—hang them on walls, doorframes, or stair railings. ### **3. Quick Decor Touches (Low-Effort, High-Impact)** - **Rangoli** (if you can, even a simple design at the entrance adds charm). For speed: - Use **colored rice flour** (pre-mixed) or **dried flowers/leaves** in a stencil. - Skip intricate designs—focus on symmetry with marigolds, turmeric, or kumkum. - **Mango leaves** (hang or place on walls/doors for auspiciousness). - **Festive fabrics**: Swap out neutral curtains/throws for **red, gold, or green** (even a single pillow cover makes a difference). - **Mirrors & glass surfaces**: Dust them and add **gold/silver rangoli dots** or **dried flowers** for sparkle. ### **4. Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. Last-Minute Essentials** - **Stock up on snacks/drinks**: Keep a tray of **laddoos, chakli, or samosas** ready for guests. - **Charge power banks** for phones/cameras (guests will want to capture the moment!). - **Prepare a welcome gesture**: A small **diya with a flower** or **mango leaf** on the doorstep for guests. ### **6. Day Before Diwali** - **Test all lights/diyas** (replace batteries if needed). - **Set out guest towels/soap** in bathrooms. - **Plan a quick photo spot** (e.g., a decorated corner with diyas and rangoli). ### **Time-Saving Tips:** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to handle one area (e.g., "You handle the kitchen diyas, I’ll do the living room"). - **Use pre-made decor**: Buy **ready-to-use rangoli colors**, **LED diya sets**, or **pre-lit garlands** from stores. - **Focus on the entrance and living room**—these are the first impressions guests will notice. ### **What to Skip (If Short on Time):** - Overly complex rangoli (even a simple line of diyas works). - Heavy, bulky decor (opt for lightweight items like fairy lights). - Perfuming the entire house (a few incense sticks or a simmer pot suffice). ### **Final Checklist (Night Before):** - [ ] All diyas are lit (or batteries charged). - [ ] Rangoli is set (even if minimal). - [ ] Entrance is welcoming (lights, mango leaves, small diya). - [ ] Snacks/drinks are ready. - [ ] Music is playing (optional but festive!). You’ve got this! Diwali is about joy, family, and warmth—so even simple decorations will feel magical. **Shubh Diwali!** 🪔✨ Would you like recommendations for specific stores or DIY hacks for any of these?

Your breakup, while valid, wasn’t the focus of the service, and asking for prayers there could feel like **stealing emotional bandwidth** from others. - **Power Dynamics:** Even if you didn’t mean to, your request might have **reinforced a hierarchy of suffering** (e.g., "Death is worse than a breakup"). It’s one thing to reflect on your values privately; it’s another to **publicly exclude someone** in a vulnerable moment. --- ### **0/1 Scale Assessment:** **Score: 0 (Not Considerate)** *(If we’re evaluating based on **intentionality, empathy, and relational impact**—not just your personal feelings.)* **Why?** - **Impact:** Your request **disrupted the emotional tone** of the service and **hurt others’ feelings**, even if unintentionally. A simple message like: *"I realize now that asking for prayers during the service was inconsiderate. I didn’t mean to overshadow others’ pain, and I’m sorry for that. I’ll be more mindful in the future."* - This shows **accountability** without over-explaining or justifying. 2. **Repair the Relationship:** - If your ex-girlfriend is open to it, you might say: *"I know my words hurt you, and I regret that. I wasn’t trying to attack you—I was just hurting. I hope we can still be friends, even if things didn’t work out."* - Give her space to respond; don’t pressure her. 3. **Process Your Pain Healthily:** - Prayer services are for **collective healing**, not personal therapy. If you need support: - Talk to a **trusted friend or mentor** outside the service. - Journal or pray **privately**. - Consider **individual counseling** if the breakup is deeply affecting you. 4. **Reflect on Boundaries:** - Your values are valid, but **how you express them matters**. Instead of saying *"only date people who share my religious values,"* you might reflect on: - *"What qualities do I need in a partner to feel secure?"* (e.g., kindness, respect, emotional availability). - *"How can I communicate my needs without making others feel excluded?"* --- ### **Final Thought:** You’re allowed to feel heartbroken, and your pain is real. But **how we ask for help—and where—matters**. A prayer service is a **sacred space for others’ healing**, not a personal support group. Your friends and ex-girlfriend’s reactions weren’t about "being unreasonable"—they were about **protecting their emotional safety**. Would you like help drafting a message to apologize to them? Or are you looking for ways to process this breakup in a healthier way?
